items.followUp: Explain two benefits of transpiration to plants.

rubric.why: Shows why transpiration may harm a plant.
rubric.description: Excessive water loss can cause wilting.
rubric.how: Award for linking water loss with wilting or another harmful effect of excessive transpiration.

rubric.why: Shows why transpiration is also important to the plant.
rubric.description: Transpiration cools the plant and helps move water and mineral salts upward.
rubric.how: Award for naming two benefits, including cooling, ascent of sap, or transport of mineral salts.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is called an evil because excessive loss of water may cause a plant to wilt.
It is necessary because it cools the plant and helps the upward movement of water and mineral salts.

items.followUp: Describe how water loss from leaves can affect a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the structures controlling the stomatal opening.
rubric.description: Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells.
rubric.how: Award for naming guard cells and the pore or stoma they surround.

rubric.why: Explains the change that leads to opening.
rubric.description: In light, water enters guard cells by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award for stating that light is associated with water entering the guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects guard-cell turgidity with the open pore.
rubric.description: The guard cells become turgid and the stomatal pore opens.
rubric.how: Award for correctly linking turgidity with opening.

rubric.why: Explains the change that leads to closing.
rubric.description: In darkness, water leaves the guard cells.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water leaves the guard cells, typically in darkness.

rubric.why: Completes the closing mechanism and illustrates the phenomenon.
rubric.description: The guard cells become flaccid and the pore closes; an illustration distinguishes open and closed stomata.
rubric.how: Award for linking flaccidity with closing, or for a clear labeled illustration showing open and closed stomata.

modelAnswer: A stoma is surrounded by two guard cells.
In light, water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, water leaves the guard cells; they become flaccid and the pore closes.
Illustration: Turgid guard cells → OPEN pore; flaccid guard cells → CLOSED pore.

items.followUp: Write down four ways in which people can help conserve biodiversity.

rubric.why: Recognizes protection of habitats and wildlife.
rubric.description: Establish protected areas such as national parks or wildlife sanctuaries.
rubric.how: Award for any valid protected-area measure.

rubric.why: Recognizes the need to prevent killing or illegal trade of organisms.
rubric.description: Enforce laws against hunting and poaching.
rubric.how: Award for a measure that controls hunting, poaching, or wildlife trade.

rubric.why: Recognizes restoration or protection of habitats.
rubric.description: Plant trees and restore natural habitats.
rubric.how: Award for afforestation, reforestation, or another valid habitat-restoration measure.

rubric.why: Recognizes another valid conservation approach.
rubric.description: Use conservation facilities or educate the public about biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award for one additional valid measure, such as seed banks, botanical gardens, zoos, or public education.

modelAnswer: Establish national parks and wildlife sanctuaries to protect habitats and species.
Enforce laws against hunting and poaching.
Plant trees and restore damaged habitats.
Conserve species in seed banks, botanical gardens, and zoos, and promote public awareness.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and two functions of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Describes the position and material of the plant cell wall.
rubric.description: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living outer covering made mainly of cellulose.
rubric.how: Award one mark for its outer, rigid, non-living nature and one for cellulose composition.

rubric.why: Identifies the cell wall's structural role.
rubric.description: It gives the cell support, protection, and shape.
rubric.how: Award for two of support, protection, or maintaining shape.

rubric.why: Identifies another important property or function.
rubric.description: It helps prevent the cell from bursting when water enters; it is freely permeable.
rubric.how: Award for preventing bursting or stating that the wall is freely permeable.

modelAnswer: The cell wall is the rigid, non-living outer covering of a plant cell.
It is made mainly of cellulose and is freely permeable.
It gives the cell shape, support, and protection.
It helps prevent the cell from bursting when water enters.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the small intestine.

rubric.why: Describes the stomach's form and general structure.
rubric.description: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the stomach as muscular and J-shaped or sac-like.

rubric.why: Locates the stomach in the digestive tract.
rubric.description: It lies between the oesophagus and the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award for correctly naming both connections.

rubric.why: Describes its secretory lining and digestive juices.
rubric.description: Its inner lining has gastric glands that secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and mucus.
rubric.how: Award for naming gastric glands and a relevant secretion or for naming two relevant components of gastric juice.

rubric.why: States a mechanical or storage function.
rubric.description: It temporarily stores food and churns it.
rubric.how: Award for storage or churning of food.

rubric.why: States a digestive function.
rubric.description: It begins protein digestion and mixes food into semi-liquid chyme.
rubric.how: Award for protein digestion or formation of chyme.

modelAnswer: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac in the upper abdomen, between the oesophagus and small intestine.
Its inner lining contains gastric glands that secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and protective mucus.
The stomach temporarily stores food and churns it, mixing it with gastric juice.
Hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium and helps kill microbes.
Pepsin begins protein digestion, and the partly digested food becomes semi-liquid chyme.

items.followUp: Define multicellular organisms and give one example.

rubric.why: States the defining feature of unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: A unicellular organism consists of a single cell that carries out all life functions.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is made of one cell and that the cell performs life functions.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example.
rubric.description: Examples include Amoeba, bacteria, Paramecium, and yeast.
rubric.how: Award for any valid unicellular organism.

modelAnswer: A unicellular organism is an organism made up of a single cell that performs all the functions of life.
Example: Amoeba.

items.followUp: How does physiology differ from morphology?

rubric.why: Defines morphology as the study of external form.
rubric.description: Morphology deals with the external form and structure of organisms.
rubric.how: Award for describing morphology as the study of external form, structure, shape, or size.

rubric.why: Defines anatomy as the study of internal structure.
rubric.description: Anatomy deals with the internal structure of organisms.
rubric.how: Award for describing anatomy as the study of internal structure or internal parts.

modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the external form and structure of an organism.
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of an organism.

items.followUp: Define tissue and give an example of a tissue.

rubric.why: Explains what an organelle is and its role in a cell.
rubric.description: An organelle is a specialized structure within a cell that performs a particular function.
rubric.how: Award for identifying it as a specialized cell structure or part with a specific function.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of an organelle.
rubric.description: Examples include mitochondrion, nucleus, chloroplast, and ribosome.
rubric.how: Award for any valid cell organelle.

modelAnswer: An organelle is a specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function.
Example: Mitochondrion.
